summary.text: Actaeon, a Theban hunter, son of Aristaeus and Autonoe the daughter of Cadmus, was devoured on Cithaeron by his own hounds — counted among the ruins that overtook the grandchildren of Cadmus.

story.text: The Theogony sets the marriage of his parents among Harmonia's children: alongside Ino, Semele, and Agave, Cadmus' daughter Autonoe is wedded by long-haired Aristaeus. The poem names the union but not the son who would spring from it.

Apollodorus and Hyginus name him plainly the son of Aristaeus and Autonoe, daughter of Cadmus, and so a grandson of Cadmus, kin to the doomed line of Thebes. He was bred to the chase and to the mountain, and the mountain undid him.

Apollodorus adds that Chiron reared him to be a hunter, and sets out the offense that doomed him three ways without settling which: according to Acusilaus, Zeus was angry at Actaeon for wooing Semele; according to the more general opinion it was because he saw Artemis bathing; and others say it was because he boasted himself a better hunter than the goddess.

Ovid tells the bathing version in full: in the vale of Gargaphie the grandson of Cadmus, wandering from the hunt, stumbled on Diana at her spring; the angry goddess flung water upon him, antlers sprang from his brow, and he fled as a stag until his own fifty hounds, blind to their master, ran him down and tore him apart.
Hyginus gives the harsher charge — that Actaeon saw Diana bathing and desired to ravish her, whereupon she set horns upon his head and his own dogs devoured him.

Pausanias preserves a regional turn from Stesichorus of Himera: that Artemis cast a deer-skin about Actaeon to make certain his hounds would tear him. At Orchomenus the dead hunter became a power: a rock-bearing ghost ravaged the land until Delphi bade the people find his remains and bury them, and fasten a bronze likeness of the ghost to a rock with iron — an image Pausanias says he saw — and thereafter they sacrificed to Actaeon every year as to a hero.
